<h1 id="halan_dashboard">halan_dashboard¶</h1><p>Name: youssef fawzy Date: 25/10/2026 Goal: to learn how to do dahsboards using pandas</p>
<h2 id="0.2-Parameters-I'll-need">0.2 Parameters I'll need¶</h2>
  • usecols: read only the columns you need
  • dtype: tell pandas the type of a column instead of letting it guess
  • parse_dates: turn date columns into real dates instead of text
<p>The variable x lived in the kernel’s memory rather than in the cell, so it survived deleting the cell, but restarting wiped the memory and Run All only re-executes the cells that still exist, so x was gone and x * 2 raised a NameError</p>
In [1]:
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick
from cycler import cycler

DATA = Path("data")
AS_OF = pd.Timestamp("2026-08-12")   # the "today" of this dataset

pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 50)
pd.set_option("display.float_format", "{:,.2f}".format)

PALETTE = ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#008300", "#6250d6", "#e34948"]
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.figsize": (10, 5), "figure.dpi": 110,
    "axes.prop_cycle": cycler(color=PALETTE),
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3, "axes.titleweight": "bold",
})

<p>Without options, pandas read customer_phone and customer_nid as int 64 , so the leading zero disappeared . With dtype=str they stay as STR and keep the 0 . This matters because phone numbers and national IDs are identifiers, not quantities: we never do maths on them,</p>
In [11]:
def read_text_ids(filename):
    path = DATA / filename
    cols = pd.read_csv(path, nrows=0).columns          # header only
    text_cols = [c for c in cols if c == "id" or c.endswith(("_id", "_phone", "_nid"))]
    print(f"{filename}: reading as text -> {text_cols}")
    return pd.read_csv(path, dtype={c: str for c in text_cols})

loans        = read_text_ids("application.csv")
installments = read_text_ids("installment.csv")
customers    = read_text_ids("customer.csv")
branches     = read_text_ids("branch.csv")
officers     = read_text_ids("officers.csv")

application.csv: reading as text -> ['loan_id', 'customer_id', 'branch_id', 'loan_officer_id']
installment.csv: reading as text -> ['installment_id', 'loan_id']
customer.csv: reading as text -> ['customer_id', 'branch_id', 'customer_phone', 'customer_nid']
branch.csv: reading as text -> ['branch_id']
officers.csv: reading as text -> ['officer_id', 'officer_nid', 'officer_phone']

<p>Their date of payment hasn’t yet arrived” is true for some of them, but not necessarily for all. Remember the date_of_payment column is the due date. Some unpaid installments could have a due date before AS_OF (2026-08-12), meaning they’re overdue, not just waiting. Either way, the reason paid_at is empty is the same: no payment has been made, so there is no payment date to record.</p>

0.72 0.28
0.72 0.28
<p>"index" divides each row by its own total, so each company’s two cells add up to 100%: it’s the write-off rate within each company. "columns" divides each column by its own total, so each column adds up to 100%: it’s each company’s share of the written-off (or not written-off) loans. The 49/51 split mirrors the 489/511 split of the portfolio, which is why the two columns look alike. "all" divides by the grand total, so the four cells add up to 100%: it’s each cell’s share of the whole portfolio.</p>

<p>pivot failed because it only rearranges values and never aggregates: each (city, company) pair appears on many rows (about 55 on average, 982 repeats in total), and pivot has no way to decide how to combine several values in one cell. pivot_table works because it has an aggfunc (for example "sum") that combines them.</p>

<p>The horizontal 100% bar is easier to read. Our eyes compare lengths on a straight line more accurately than angles and areas on a donut, and the percentages sit next to each other on the same scale. This matters here because the two shares are close (CF about 48% and MICRO about 52%): on the donut the difference is hard to see, while on the bar it is clear at a glance. A donut is fine for a quick overview, but not for comparing close values.</p>

# ---------- 1. The function: the nine KPIs for any loans/installments pair ----------
def kpis(df_loans, df_inst):
    act_l = df_loans[(df_loans["loan_status"] == "issued") & (~df_loans["write_off"])]
    act_i = df_inst[(df_inst["loan_status"] == "issued") & (~df_inst["write_off"])]

    d = df_inst[df_inst["is_due"]]
    exp = d["installment_response"].sum()
    col = d["total_paid"].sum()

    unpaid = d[d["installment_status"] != "paid"]
    oldest = unpaid.groupby("loan_id")["date_of_payment"].min()
    days = (AS_OF - oldest).dt.days

    per_loan = act_i.groupby("loan_id")["outstanding_principal"].sum().to_frame("outstanding")
    per_loan["dpd"] = days.reindex(per_loan.index)
    total_out = per_loan["outstanding"].sum()

    return pd.Series({
        "Active loans": len(act_l),
        "Active customers": act_l["customer_id"].nunique(),
        "Active outstanding": total_out,
        "Expected": exp,
        "Collected": col,
        "Collection rate": col / exp,
        "Arrears": exp - col,
        "PAR 30": per_loan.loc[per_loan["dpd"] > 30, "outstanding"].sum() / total_out,
        "PAR 90": per_loan.loc[per_loan["dpd"] > 90, "outstanding"].sum() / total_out,
    })

# ---------- 2. Call it once per company, plus the whole portfolio ----------
by_function = pd.DataFrame({
    c: kpis(loans_full[loans_full["company"] == c],
            installments_full[installments_full["company"] == c])
    for c in ["CF", "MICRO"]
})
by_function["Total"] = kpis(loans_full, installments_full)

# ---------- 3. The same KPIs with groupby ----------
al = loans_full[(loans_full["loan_status"] == "issued") & (~loans_full["write_off"])]
ai = installments_full[(installments_full["loan_status"] == "issued") & (~installments_full["write_off"])]
dd = installments_full[installments_full["is_due"]]

g = pd.DataFrame({
    "Active loans": al.groupby("company").size(),
    "Active customers": al.groupby("company")["customer_id"].nunique(),
    "Active outstanding": ai.groupby("company")["outstanding_principal"].sum(),
    "Expected": dd.groupby("company")["installment_response"].sum(),
    "Collected": dd.groupby("company")["total_paid"].sum(),
})
g["Collection rate"] = g["Collected"] / g["Expected"]
g["Arrears"] = g["Expected"] - g["Collected"]

unpaid_dd = dd[dd["installment_status"] != "paid"]
days_g = (AS_OF - unpaid_dd.groupby("loan_id")["date_of_payment"].min()).dt.days
pl = ai.groupby("loan_id")["outstanding_principal"].sum().to_frame("outstanding")
pl["dpd"] = days_g.reindex(pl.index)
pl["company"] = loans_full.set_index("loan_id")["company"].reindex(pl.index)

tot = pl.groupby("company")["outstanding"].sum()
g["PAR 30"] = (pl[pl["dpd"] > 30].groupby("company")["outstanding"].sum() / tot).fillna(0)
g["PAR 90"] = (pl[pl["dpd"] > 90].groupby("company")["outstanding"].sum() / tot).fillna(0)

by_groupby = g.T.reindex(by_function.index)[["CF", "MICRO"]]

# ---------- 4. Checks ----------
print("Max difference function vs groupby:",
      (by_function[["CF", "MICRO"]] - by_groupby).abs().max().max())
print("Total column matches 6.1 (active loans, collection rate):",
      by_function.loc["Active loans", "Total"], f"{by_function.loc['Collection rate', 'Total']:.1%}")

# ---------- 5. Nicely formatted display ----------
rates = ["Collection rate", "PAR 30", "PAR 90"]
shown = by_function.astype(object)
for kpi in shown.index:
    for column in shown.columns:
        v = by_function.loc[kpi, column]
        shown.loc[kpi, column] = f"{v:.1%}" if kpi in rates else f"{v:,.0f}"
shown

<p>MICRO collects slightly better than CF (57.8% against 55.7%) and has a lower PAR 30 (64.2% against 66.8%), but its PAR 90 is a bit higher (60.5% against 59.2%). Both companies have a similar amount of arrears (about 3.8 million each), so neither is clearly riskier: the differences are only a few points.</p> <p>The PAR values are very high (about 65% at 30 days and 60% at 90 days). This comes from the definition: when a loan is late, its whole remaining balance counts as at risk, including installments that are not yet due, and the collection rate overall is only 56.8%. These figures are much higher than what a healthy lender would report, so they describe this dataset and this definition and not a general benchmark.</p>
